levels.title: Guess the Tide
levels.story: Tide Clerk Toby keeps a long sorted chart of tide heights. Visitors ask whether a certain height ever happened, and Toby can answer in a few glances.

everyday.scene: I am thinking of a number from 1 to 100. You may ask yes-or-no questions like "is it more than 50?".
everyday.question: How many questions do you need, at most?
everyday.answer: Seven. Each answer cuts the choices in half: 100, 50, 25, 13, 7, 4, 2, 1. That is exactly how binary search works.

lessons.title: Solve a smaller copy
text: Recursion means solving a problem by solving a smaller copy of the same problem. A recursive method needs two parts: a base case, which is small enough to answer directly, and a step that shrinks the problem and calls the method again.
Example: the sum of 1 to n is n plus the sum of 1 to n − 1. The base case is that the sum up to 0 is 0. Each call is smaller than the one before, so the chain must end at the base case.

terms.meaning: A method that calls itself on a smaller problem.
A problem so small it is answered directly.

predict.prompt: What does a recursive method return when it reaches the base case?
predict.answer: A direct answer, with no more calls.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

lessons.title: Throw away half
text: Binary search finds a value in a sorted list. Look at the middle item. If it is the one you want, stop. If it is too small, the answer can only be in the right half. If it is too big, only in the left half. Throw the other half away and repeat.
This only works because the list is sorted. Without order, one look tells you nothing about the rest. The list shrinks by half each time, so it is a 'decrease by a factor' method.

terms.meaning: Find a value in a sorted list by repeatedly checking the middle.

predict.prompt: A sorted list has 15 items, and the middle is too small. How many items remain to search?
predict.answer: At most 7: everything to the right of the middle.

lessons.title: How many halvings?
text: Each check halves the list, so the number of checks is how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, plus one. That is floor(log₂ n) + 1. For 1,000 items it is 10. For a million it is 20. For a billion it is 30.
Compare with scanning from the left: a billion checks in the worst case. Doubling the list adds only one more check. That is what 'logarithmic growth' feels like: almost flat.

predict.prompt: If you double the list, how many more checks does binary search need at most?

activities.prompt: Watch binary search look for 58 among 15 sorted heights, and predict each decision.

feed.explain: Sorted order lets one check discard half.

Name the two parts every recursive method needs.
feed.answer: A base case that answers directly, and a step that calls the method on a smaller problem.

The list stays the same size

fieldNotes.title: Looking things up in sorted data
fieldNotes.text: Whenever data is kept in sorted order, a program can find an item by halving instead of scanning. Some libraries include a ready-made version, such as Python's bisect module, which keeps a list in sorted order and finds positions by bisection.

summary: You met recursion with a base case, watched binary search discard half the chart at each look, and saw that a billion items take only about 30 checks.
Toby nods. "Sorted data is a gift: keep it sorted and every question is cheap."

mistake.title: Using binary search on an unsorted list
mistake.text: Binary search gives wrong answers on unsorted data, because discarding half assumes order. Sort first, or use a different method.

levels.title: Power Shell
levels.story: Painter Pia has found a magic shell that triples every time she taps it. She needs 3 to a very big power, and does not want to tap a thousand times.

everyday.scene: You need to fold a sheet in half 20 times to see how thick it gets. Folding 20 times is 20 jobs. But suppose you wanted 2²⁰ copies: do you really need 19 multiplications?
everyday.question: Can you reach a power with fewer multiplications than the exponent?
everyday.answer: Yes. By squaring, you reach 2²⁰ in 5 multiplications. The big idea: use the answer for half the size, and square it.

lessons.title: The slow way
text: To compute aⁿ the simple way, multiply a by itself n − 1 times. This is a decrease-by-one method: aⁿ = a × aⁿ⁻¹. It is correct and clear, but needs n − 1 multiplications, so a million-power needs nearly a million steps.
With big numbers, each multiplication is itself slow. A method with far fewer multiplications is worth a lot, and a good idea is waiting in the shell.

predict.prompt: How many multiplications does the plain method need for a¹⁰⁰?

lessons.title: Square the half
text: If the exponent n is even, aⁿ = (aⁿ/²)². So find aⁿ/² (one smaller problem, half the size), then square it with one multiplication. If n is odd, aⁿ = a × aⁿ⁻¹, and then n − 1 is even, so it halves next.
The base case is a¹ = a. For 3¹³, the exponents go 13, 12, 6, 3, 2, 1. That is 5 multiplications in total, against 12 for the plain method.

predict.prompt: What is a⁸ if you know a⁴?

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

lessons.title: Counting the multiplications
text: Every exponent halves at least every second step, so the number of calls is about 2 × log₂ n at most. For n = 1,000 the fast method needs 14 multiplications, not 999. For n = 1,000,000 it needs 25.

The plain method grows in step with n. Squaring grows in step with the number of digits of n, which barely moves. In decrease-and-conquer language, this is a decrease-by-half method, like binary search.

predict.prompt: Is the speed of the squaring method closer to n or to the number of digits of n?
predict.answer: The number of digits of n. The exponent is halved at each step.

activities.prompt: Watch 3¹³ get computed by squaring. Predict the answers as they come back.

steps.say: Kit wants 3¹³. The recursive plan: if the exponent is even, square the answer for half of it. If odd, multiply by 3 once and use the exponent one smaller.
3^13 needs 3^12 (odd: one exponent less). A new call waits.
3^12 needs 3^6 (even: half the exponent). A new call waits.
3^6 needs 3^3 (even: half the exponent). A new call waits.
3^3 needs 3^2 (odd: one exponent less). A new call waits.
3^2 needs 3^1 (even: half the exponent). A new call waits.
3^1 is the base case: the answer is 3.
3^2 = 3^1 squared = 9.

hints: The exponent is even: square the previous answer.

predict.prompt: Answers coming back: 3^2 = 9. What is 3^3?
hints: The exponent is odd: multiply by 3 once.

predict.prompt: Answers coming back: 3^3 = 27. What is 3^6?
hints: The exponent is even: square the previous answer.

predict.prompt: Answers coming back: 3^6 = 729. What is 3^12?
hints: The exponent is even: square the previous answer.

predict.prompt: Answers coming back: 3^12 = 531,441. What is 3^13?
hints: The exponent is odd: multiply by 3 once.

activities.explain: Watch 3¹³ get computed by squaring. Predict the answers as they come back.

activities.prompt: How many multiplications does the squaring method use for 3¹³?
hints: Count the calls other than the base case. Each one does one multiplication.
The exponents are 13, 12, 6, 3, 2, 1.
activities.explain: One multiplication in each of the 5 calls above the base case: 5.

activities.prompt: How many multiplications does the squaring method use for a¹⁰⁰⁰?
hints: Follow the exponent: 1000 even, 500 even, 250 even, 125 odd, 124 even...
Count the odd steps and the even steps.
activities.explain: The exponents go 1000, 500, 250, 125, 124, 62, 31, 30, 15, 14, 7, 6, 3, 2, 1: 14 steps that each multiply once.

activities.prompt: To compute a¹⁶ when you know a⁸, you...
hints: Think about the exponents: 8 + 8.
a⁸ × a⁸ = a¹⁶, which is a⁸ squared.
activities.explain: Squaring doubles the exponent: (a⁸)² = a¹⁶.

activities.prompt: The exponents visited when computing 3¹³ are:
hints: An odd exponent goes to the number one smaller.
An even exponent goes to half of it.
activities.explain: From 13 (odd) to 12, then half to 6, half to 3, odd to 2, half to 1.

activities.prompt: Challenge: how many multiplications does the squaring method use for a¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰?
hints: Roughly twice the number of halvings of a million, at most.
Halving a million down to 1 takes 19 steps.
activities.explain: It takes 19 halvings plus a multiplication for each odd step: 25.

activities.prompt: Challenge: what is 3¹³?
hints: 3⁶ squared times 3.

feed.prompt: What do you do when the exponent is odd?
feed.answer: Multiply by a once, then use the exponent one smaller (which is even).

feed.prompt: Squaring needs far fewer multiplications because...

options.text: The exponent roughly halves at each step

feed.explain: Halving the exponent is the whole saving.

fieldNotes.title: Powers in secure messaging
fieldNotes.text: Public-key cryptography, including RSA and Diffie–Hellman, depends on modular exponentiation: raising big numbers to big powers and keeping only the remainder. It stays efficient even for very large numbers, and squaring methods like this one are a standard way to do it.

summary: You computed 3¹³ by squaring in 5 multiplications instead of 12, and saw the saving grow as the exponent gets large.
Pia taps the shell once and grins. "The trick was to ask what half the job looks like." Halving appears again and again in fast methods.

mistake.title: Squaring when the exponent is odd
mistake.text: Squaring only works when you halve an even exponent. For an odd one, multiply by a first to make the exponent even.

levels.title: Recipe Order
levels.story: Baker Bea has a cake to make, and some jobs must happen before others: no baking before mixing, and no cooling before baking. Kit has to find an order that respects all of it.

everyday.scene: You are getting ready for a trip: pack the bag, but the bag cannot be packed until the washing is dry, and the washing cannot be dried until it is washed.
everyday.question: How do you find an order of jobs that never breaks a "before" rule?
everyday.answer: Do any job that is waiting for nothing, cross it off, and look again. That simple loop is called a topological sort.

lessons.title: Jobs with "before" rules
text: Some jobs depend on others. We draw each job as a dot and each rule 'A must come before B' as an arrow from A to B. A picture with arrows like this is a directed graph, and here it shows prerequisites.
A valid order puts every job after all jobs that have an arrow into it. Usually there are several valid orders. Our recipe has 8 of them, and any one is fine to follow.

terms.meaning: Dots joined by arrows that point one way.
A job that must be finished first.

predict.prompt: Jobs A, B, C with arrows A → B and B → C. How many valid orders are there?

lessons.title: Remove what is ready
text: The method is decrease by one. Find a job with no unfinished prerequisite. Put it next in the order, then cross it off. That makes the problem one job smaller. Repeat until nothing is left.
Every time, at least one job must be ready, unless there is a cycle. A cycle means jobs wait for each other in a ring, as in 'pack after dry, dry after pack', and then no order exists at all.

terms.meaning: Putting jobs in an order that respects every "before" rule.
A ring of jobs that each wait for the next.

predict.prompt: At some point, jobs are left but none is ready. What does that tell you?
predict.answer: There is a cycle, so no valid order exists.

deeper.title: Another way
text: A depth-first search can also build a valid order. You will see depth-first search on the Bridge Isles.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 6: Depth-First Search

lessons.title: Many answers, one rule
text: The answer is rarely unique. In our recipe, Flour and Eggs can go in either order, and Oven can go at many points. All 8 orders work, and none is the best unless there are extra rules like time.

Topological sorting is how build tools decide which files to compile first, and how course planners order subjects. The arrows are the only input. The method finds an order, and warns when none can exist.

predict.prompt: Two jobs are both ready. Does it matter which you do first?
predict.answer: No. Either choice leaves a valid order, since neither waits for the other.

fieldNotes.title: Build tools and course plans
fieldNotes.text: Software build tools work out an order in which to compile files so that each file is built after the files it needs. The same idea orders subjects when some are prerequisites for others.

summary: You turned "before" rules into arrows, repeatedly removed ready jobs, and found that a cycle means no order exists.
Bea ties her apron. "Flour, eggs, mix, oven, bake, cool." The cake is on its way, and the recipe card is back in order.

mistake.title: Starting with any job
mistake.text: You cannot start with a job that still has unfinished prerequisites. Start with a job nothing is waiting for.

levels.title: The Partition Pier
levels.story: Dock Clerk Dot has to find the middle crate by weight without sorting the whole pile. She uses a pivot crate, and only works on the side that matters.

everyday.scene: In a shuffled queue of 101 people you need to find the median height. Sorting everyone takes a lot of lining up.
everyday.question: Is there a way to find the middle person without lining everyone up?
everyday.answer: Yes. Pick someone, split everyone into shorter and taller, and then look only at the side that holds the middle. That trick is called quickselect.

lessons.title: Split around a pivot
text: Partitioning picks one crate, the pivot, and rearranges the row so smaller crates sit on its left and bigger ones on its right. The pivot then sits in its final sorted place, even though the rest are not sorted.

The version here uses the last crate as the pivot. It walks along the row, and every crate smaller than the pivot is swapped into a growing left part. For 31, 12, 45, 8, 27, 19, 36, the pivot 36 ends at position 5. It takes 6 comparisons, one for each other crate.

terms.meaning: The crate that the others are compared with.
Rearrange so smaller ones are left of the pivot and bigger ones right.

predict.prompt: A row of 9 crates is partitioned. How many comparisons with the pivot?
predict.answer: 8. Every other crate is compared once.

lessons.title: Keep only one side
text: To find the 4th smallest crate, partition, and look at where the pivot lands. If the pivot lands at position 3 (counting from 0), it is the answer. If it lands too far right, the answer is on the left. If too far left, the answer is on the right. Throw away the other side.
This is decrease and conquer with a variable decrease: the amount thrown away depends on where the pivot lands. Unlike sorting, you only continue with one side.

terms.meaning: Find the kth smallest item by partitioning and keeping only the side that holds it.

predict.prompt: The pivot lands at position 2, and you want the item at position 5. Which side do you keep?
predict.answer: The right side. Position 5 is beyond the pivot.

lessons.title: What it costs
text: On a lucky split, each round halves the row, so the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... which adds up to about 2n comparisons. That is about as good as scanning the row once or twice, and far less than sorting.

On a very unlucky split, such as always picking the largest crate, each round throws away just one crate, and the total is about n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 comparisons. Choosing the pivot well, for example at random, makes bad luck rare.

predict.prompt: Why might a very bad pivot choice make quickselect slow?
predict.answer: It throws away only one crate each round, so there are almost n rounds.

deeper.title: The guaranteed method
text: There is a more complicated way to choose the pivot that guarantees work proportional to n in the worst case. It is rarely used in practice because the simple random method is faster on average.

fieldNotes.title: Medians in the real world
fieldNotes.text: Finding a median, such as the typical response time, is an everyday job in data analysis. Selection algorithms such as quickselect find the k-th smallest value, the median included, in linear time on average, which beats sorting everything first.

summary: You partitioned a row around a pivot, saw that the pivot lands in its final place, and used that to throw away a whole side when looking for the 4th smallest.
Dot hands over the middle crate. "No full sort needed." The same partition idea powers quicksort, which you will meet on Split Rock.

mistake.title: Thinking the left and right sides are sorted
mistake.text: Partition only guarantees that smaller crates are on the left and bigger ones on the right. Inside each side, the order is still mixed.
